title: Companies That Treat Service as a Cost Center Are Giving Away Their Moat
dek: Products get replaced by better products, brands by stronger brands; the only durable competitive advantage is hospitality — the continuous, generous investment in relationships.
why: This is an interview with Will Guidara about Unreasonable Hospitality. No AI or fundraising takeaways, but it nails "service as moat" — worth listening to as a way of thinking about running a business.
who: Founders and early-stage investors building products, building services, leading teams — especially anyone treating customer support as a cost center and looking for a moat beyond the product.
skip: If you don't care about restaurant-operations detail, the segment after 51:00 on Toast, tipping and reservation scalpers can be skipped.

points.h: Product moats get filled in sooner or later
points.body: Guidara's argument: most companies are looking for their moat, and the traditional answer is to build the best product and the strongest brand. But he thinks those only work up to a point, because time has repeatedly shown that sooner or later someone builds a better product and a stronger brand — they may have more capital, more creativity, new ideas, or they're simply better than you. So he thinks the only competitive advantage that exists over the long term comes from hospitality, from continuously and generously investing in relationships. This isn't to say making a great product doesn't matter; it's that you shouldn't reserve your best effort only for the product — you should also invest in how people feel.

points.h: The front line has information and no power; leadership has power and no information
points.body: Guidara quotes retired Navy captain David Marquet: in most organizations, senior leadership has all the power and no information, while the front line has all the information and no power. His inference: you cannot deliver unreasonable hospitality without empowering the front line, because only the people on the front line know the guest well enough to know what would make this particular service "unreasonable." His book covers feedback methods, the daily 30-minute meeting, how to celebrate and create traditions the team looks forward to — but he says the greatest unreasonable hospitality you can give your colleagues is to genuinely give them agency.

points.h: Hospitality can be systematized, not just a flash of inspiration
points.body: One-off gestures like the hot dog or the first dance are hard to scale — they need someone to come up with them in the moment, and forcing them looks contrived. But Guidara says these are exactly what proves hospitality can be systematized: do pattern recognition, find the moments that recur, then write "how we respond when this moment happens" into the process. For example, guests used to constantly need to feed the parking meter, so the rule became: every time it comes up, go top up the meter for the guest. His key observation is that once hospitality is written into the system, it actually makes the team want to be hospitable even more — because every time you see the look on a guest's face when they're taken care of, that feeling is addictive.

points.h: A crying baby on a plane is a hundred-dollar bill nobody picks up
points.body: Guidara gives an example he considers "criminal": flying across the US with a one-year-old is excruciating, and it happens every single day, yet no airline has ever done anything about it — no earplugs handed out to nearby passengers, no help offered to the parent trying to soothe the baby, and milk is always out. He says this is an opportunity sitting right there in pattern recognition, a case of "there's a hundred dollars on the ground and you don't pick it up." Jason then adds the mechanism: you need top leadership to provide a budget — say, $250 a month per flight attendant to spend at their discretion doing something for the guest — so employees fall in love with their jobs and guests become loyal customers.

points.h: Hospitality shouldn't be an extra; it should be standard
points.body: Guidara says the top level not only has to give people a budget to do things beyond expectations, but also has to create a culture where this is no longer treated as "beyond expectations" but as normal. His analogy: when you buy a car, everyone assumes it comes with tires — nobody thinks of that as an extra service; phones now ship without a charger, and that too was someone deciding this step went too far. So why can't an airline decide "this flight just includes these things"? His conclusion: if you run a company, hospitality should be put into table stakes, not treated as optional.

points.h: Refunding a bag of dog food when the pet dies buys a customer for life
points.body: Guidara tells the Chewy example: dog food is an auto-subscription, and when a dog dies, the owner's first thought usually isn't to cancel the subscription — they only remember when the next bag arrives, which is cruel. When you call Chewy to cancel and return the bag, the response is always the same: we can't take the food back, but we'll refund you, just donate it. Then within a day or two, flowers arrive at that home. Guidara's inference: this person will get another dog, and where they buy dog food goes without saying — and they'll never consider anyone else. He calls this "pattern recognition, recurring moments, systematizing kindness."

points.h: Ending tipping requires a business strong enough to absorb it
points.body: Guidara eliminated tipping at Eleven Madison Park. He says it was the most successful no-tipping implementation, but after he sold the restaurant it was reinstated, because the restaurant wasn't performing as well as before. His judgment: eliminating tipping requires you to run the business extremely well, otherwise it backfires. Two preconditions must hold — first, demand must be high enough that guests don't mind higher prices to cover the absence of tipping, because the public will still compare your chicken to other restaurants' chicken without factoring in the tip they'd pay elsewhere; second, you must stay consistently full, because you're covering the team's tips yourself, and one slow night means you eat the loss directly. His approach wasn't to add a service charge but to fold service directly into the fixed tasting-menu price.

points.h: Commuter rail hides a minute of grace
points.body: Guidara shares a discovery he recently wrote up in his newsletter: commuter rail systems like Metro-North and Amtrak have a built-in "minute of grace" — the timetable says 11:45 departure, but it always actually leaves at 11:46, precisely to leave time for the person sprinting through the doors at the last second. He says he used to think sliding through the doors just in time was luck every time; once he knew it was deliberate design, he started looking for places to add a "minute of grace" in his own work with other companies. He treats this as a takeaway operating principle: where can you add a little more grace?
